subsection: 4. Reform movements in Eastern Europe, the collapse of the Soviet Union, and fragmentation and realignment, 1953–1992

notes.h: The Soviet bloc and the pressures for reform
notes.b: After 1945 the Soviet Union kept control of eastern Europe through communist parties loyal to Moscow. Reform movements kept appearing inside this system, and knowing how it held together explains why they were suppressed for so long and then succeeded so quickly.
points: Communism, as practised in the Soviet bloc, meant rule by a single communist party and a state-owned, centrally planned economy. It is the system that reformers tried to change and that collapsed in 1989-91.

The bloc consisted of one-party 'satellite' states (formally independent countries controlled by Moscow): Poland, Czechoslovakia, Hungary, Romania, Bulgaria and East Germany. Soviet troops were stationed in several of them, so the control was real and not just a matter of influence.
Two alliances tied the satellites to the USSR: Comecon (1949), an economic alliance, and the Warsaw Pact (1955), a military alliance.

The Soviet leaders in order were Stalin (died March 1953), Khrushchev (removed 1964), Leonid Brezhnev (1964-82), Yuri Andropov (1982-84), Konstantin Chernenko (1984-85) and Mikhail Gorbachev (1985-91).
Hungary in 1956 was the standing warning: a reform movement that left the Warsaw Pact was crushed by Soviet tanks, so every later reformer knew how far Moscow would go.

By the 1970s and 1980s the command economy (where the state plans production instead of the market) brought shortages, low living standards, stagnation and, in Poland, heavy foreign debt, which steadily cost the regimes public support.

The Helsinki Final Act of 1975, signed by the USA, Canada and almost all European states, East and West, contained human-rights commitments. Dissidents (open critics of the regime) later used them against their own governments.

In the early 1980s came a 'second Cold War': the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan (December 1979), then Ronald Reagan, US president 1981-89, called the USSR an 'evil empire' (1983) and announced the Strategic Defense Initiative ('Star Wars') in 1983, raising the cost of the arms race.

notes.h: Early reform movements: East Germany and Poland, 1953-1956
notes.b: Within a few years of Stalin's death, workers in two satellite states challenged their governments. How Moscow answered each one set a pattern that lasted until 1968.
points: On 17 June 1953 building workers in East Berlin protested against increased work norms (more work for the same pay, in effect a wage cut). With shortages and Stalin's death in March, the protests spread to hundreds of towns across East Germany.

Soviet tanks put the rising down, so it failed, and dozens were killed (no reliable exact figure). Walter Ulbricht, the East German communist leader, stayed in power, and emigration westward continued until the Berlin Wall closed the border.
In June 1956 workers protested in Poznań, Poland, because of poor conditions, and the army put the protest down, killing dozens (no exact figure).
In October 1956 Władysław Gomułka, a communist purged in 1948-49, became party First Secretary after Khrushchev and other Soviet leaders flew to Warsaw. Soviet troops moved but did not intervene.
Moscow held back because Poland stayed in the Warsaw Pact and the party kept control of the country, so the change of leader did not threaten Soviet interests.

Gomułka ended forced collectivisation (most farms returned to private hands), released Cardinal Stefan Wyszyński from internment and gave the Church and intellectuals more freedom, though the party kept one-party rule.
By the 1960s Gomułka had tightened controls again, so the 1956 settlement proved limited because the party never gave up its monopoly.
The pattern was Poland 1956 (concession), Hungary 1956 (crushed) and Czechoslovakia 1968 (invaded): reform was tolerated only if the party kept its monopoly and the country stayed in the Pact.
notes.tip: If asked how successful Soviet control of eastern Europe was, date each crisis (1953, 1956, 1968) and judge that control was kept by force, never by consent. Keep Gomułka (1956-70), Gierek (1970-80) and Jaruzelski (1981-89) apart.

notes.h: The Prague Spring, 1968
notes.b: In Czechoslovakia in 1968 reform came from inside the communist party itself. The reformers wanted 'socialism with a human face' (communism made freer and more humane), but their Warsaw Pact allies ended the experiment by force.
points: Czechoslovakia had a hardline leader, Antonin Novotný, a stagnant economy and Slovak grievances. On 5 January 1968 the Slovak Alexander Dubček replaced Novotný as First Secretary of the party, which opened the way to reform.

The Action Programme of April 1968 proposed freedom of speech and the press, the rehabilitation (official clearing of the names) of victims of the 1950s and curbs on the secret police. Censorship ended in practice in spring 1968.

Dubček's government also planned economic reform with market mechanisms and a federal settlement for Czechs and Slovaks. The federal republics were agreed in 1968 and took effect on 1 January 1969, the one reform that survived.
In June 1968 the writer Ludvík Vaculík's 'Two Thousand Words' manifesto urged faster reform.

Dubček did not propose leaving the Warsaw Pact or ending communism: he insisted that Czechoslovakia stayed in the Pact and that the party kept its leading role. This is the key difference from Imre Nagy's step in Hungary in 1956.

Soviet leaders feared that reform would spread to Poland, East Germany and Ukraine. In July 1968 the Soviet, East German, Polish, Hungarian and Bulgarian leaders sent the Warsaw Letter of warning, and talks followed at Čierna nad Tisou and Bratislava in late July and early August.
On the night of 20-21 August 1968 Soviet, Polish, Hungarian and Bulgarian forces invaded Czechoslovakia. East German troops were prepared but kept back, apart from a token presence.

Dubček and other leaders were seized and flown to Moscow and forced to sign the Moscow Protocol. Resistance was mainly passive, such as removing street signs and talking to the soldiers, so there was little fighting.
notes.tip: Do not say Dubček wanted to leave the Warsaw Pact or end communism; leaving the Pact was Nagy's step in 1956. Name the four invading states and say East German troops were kept back.

notes.h: The Brezhnev Doctrine, normalisation and Charter 77
notes.b: The invasion split the communist world and gave Moscow a justification for intervening again. Inside Czechoslovakia it was followed by a hard-line clean-up, while a small dissident movement kept the ideas of reform alive.
points: Romania, under Nicolae Ceaușescu, refused to take part in the invasion and condemned it, and Albania formally left the Warsaw Pact in September 1968 in protest.

The Brezhnev Doctrine was set out in a Pravda article on 26 September 1968 and in Brezhnev's speech to the Polish party congress in November. It held that when socialism is threatened in one socialist country, it is the concern of all, so Moscow claimed a right to intervene.

Normalisation (the restoration of strict party control) followed. Gustáv Husák replaced Dubček as First Secretary in April 1969, and hundreds of thousands of party members were expelled or left in the purges.
Dubček himself was expelled from the party in 1970 and worked as a forestry official, which shows how completely the reformers were removed.
In January 1969 the student Jan Palach set himself on fire in Prague in protest at the crushing of reform, and died days later.

Charter 77, published in January 1977, demanded that the government respect the human rights it had signed up to in the Helsinki Final Act of 1975 and in UN covenants. Dissidents were using the regime's own promises against it.
Its first spokesmen were Václav Havel, Jan Patočka and Jiří Hájek, so it had no single leader.
Havel, a playwright and the Charter's best-known figure, was imprisoned several times, the longest term being 1979-83. Charter 77 mattered because it kept reform alive through years of repression.
notes.tip: Prague 1968 is a turning point in Cold War questions: explain why the Brezhnev Doctrine changed the direction of events, not just what happened. Say Havel was one of Charter 77's spokesmen, not its leader.

notes.h: Key personality: Pope John Paul II (political role)
notes.b: Karol Wojtyła, elected pope in 1978, gave moral support to the Polish opposition to communism and so became a political figure as well as a religious leader. Here we cover only his political role.
points: Born in Wadowice, Poland, in 1920, Karol Wojtyła became Archbishop of Kraków in 1964 and a cardinal in 1967. He was elected pope on 16 October 1978, taking the name John Paul II, the first non-Italian pope since Adrian VI (1522-23).

His first visit to Poland as pope, 2-10 June 1979, drew huge crowds. At the open-air Mass in Victory Square, Warsaw, on 2 June he prayed: 'Let your Spirit descend, and renew the face of the earth, the face of this land.'
The visit showed Poles that they were many and could organise independently of the state, and many took his prayer for the renewal of their land as encouragement to demand change.
In August 1980 the pope's picture hung on the Gdańsk shipyard gate during the strike, which shows that his election and visit had given many Poles the confidence to organise.

He returned to Poland in June 1983, when he met Lech Wałęsa, and in June 1987. His sermons defended workers' rights and human dignity without calling for revolt, which gave Solidarity moral support while the authorities tried to suppress it.
He was shot in St Peter's Square, Rome, on 13 May 1981 by Mehmet Ali Ağca, a Turkish gunman, and recovered. Claims of Bulgarian or Soviet involvement have never been proven.

The Polish and Soviet governments saw him as a threat, and the Polish secret police monitored the Church closely. On 1 December 1989 he received Gorbachev in the Vatican, the first Soviet Communist Party leader (General Secretary) to meet a pope.

Historians debate how far he caused 1989: many see a moral leader who strengthened Polish civil society (groups organised outside the state), others stress economic and Soviet factors. Gorbachev wrote in 1992 that events in eastern Europe would have been impossible without the pope.
notes.tip: Higher answers need a judgement on how far he caused the fall of communism, set against economic and Soviet factors; treat his role as a debated judgement, not a proven cause. Say the Gorbachev meeting was the first with a Soviet Communist Party leader, not with any Soviet leader.

notes.h: Poland: the rise of Solidarity, 1980
notes.b: Poland's economic troubles produced the first independent trade union in the Soviet bloc. Solidarity grew from a shipyard strike into a national movement, forcing the communist state to deal with an organised opposition.
points: In December 1970 price rises caused strikes on the Baltic coast (Gdańsk, Gdynia, Szczecin); troops fired on workers and Gomułka was replaced by Edward Gierek. Gierek borrowed heavily from the West in the 1970s, protests followed price rises in 1976, and meat-price rises came in July 1980.
The strike at the Lenin Shipyard in Gdańsk began on 14 August 1980, sparked by the sacking of the crane operator Anna Walentynowicz.
The inter-factory strike committee made 21 demands, including free trade unions, the right to strike, the release of political prisoners, access to the media and better supplies.
The Gdańsk Agreement, signed on 31 August 1980, gave the strikers the right to form free trade unions and to strike, a concession forced on the state by the strike.
Solidarity (Solidarność) was founded in September 1980 and registered by the courts in November 1980. Its leader was Lech Wałęsa, an electrician at the shipyard who had been sacked in 1976.

At its peak in 1981 it had about ten million members, about a quarter of the population, and Rural Solidarity was formed for farmers in 1981. With Church and intellectual support, this made it a national movement rather than just a union.
notes.tip: Keep the dates apart: Gdańsk Agreement 31 August 1980, Solidarity founded September 1980, martial law 13 December 1981, Solidarity legalised again April 1989.

notes.h: Martial law, underground Solidarity and the Round Table, 1981-1989
notes.b: The state struck back in December 1981, but it could not destroy Solidarity. Eight years later the same regime had to negotiate with it.
points: General Wojciech Jaruzelski, prime minister from February 1981 and party First Secretary from October 1981, declared martial law on 13 December 1981. Wałęsa and other Solidarity leaders were interned, the union was suspended, and a curfew and army rule through the Military Council of National Salvation followed.
The union was formally banned in October 1982 so that it could not revive, and martial law was lifted in July 1983.

Jaruzelski later claimed martial law was the 'lesser evil' that prevented a Soviet invasion. Moscow had pressed for firm action, but Soviet Politburo records from December 1981 suggest it was unwilling to send troops.

Historians still debate how to read those records and whether the invasion threat was real, and many add that Jaruzelski also acted to keep communist control. Martial law was control by proxy: Poles, not Soviet troops, did the repressing.

Wałęsa was released in November 1982 and won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1983. Father Jerzy Popiełuszko, a pro-Solidarity priest, was murdered by secret police officers in October 1984, and the officers were tried and convicted.
Strike waves in 1988 showed that Solidarity's support had survived the years of repression, which is why the government had to talk to it.

Round Table talks between the government and the Solidarity-led opposition ran from 6 February to 5 April 1989. They agreed partly free elections (a set share of Sejm, the lower house, seats reserved for the communists and their allies, and a new freely elected Senate) and a new presidency.
Solidarity was legalised again on 17 April 1989, which opened the way to the June elections because it could now stand candidates.
notes.tip: On martial law, give both views: Jaruzelski's 'lesser evil' claim and the evidence that Moscow was unwilling to send troops. Present it as a debate, not settled fact.

notes.h: Key personality: Mikhail Gorbachev
notes.b: Mikhail Gorbachev, Soviet leader from 1985, began reforms that he meant to renew socialism but that ended with the collapse of communist rule in eastern Europe and the break-up of the USSR.
points: He was born on 2 March 1931 in Privolnoye, in the Stavropol region, to a peasant family. He took a law degree at Moscow State University (1955), where he met his wife Raisa.

He rose through the party in Stavropol (regional First Secretary in 1970), became Central Committee secretary for agriculture in 1978 and a full Politburo member in 1980, as a protege of Yuri Andropov.

He became General Secretary on 11 March 1985, on Chernenko's death, as the youngest Politburo member. He was head of state from October 1988 (chairman of the Presidium of the Supreme Soviet), chairman of the new Supreme Soviet in 1989 and President of the USSR in March 1990.

He was chosen by the party in 1985 and by the Congress of People's Deputies in 1990, never by popular vote; Boris Yeltsin, elected in June 1991, was the one with a popular mandate. Gorbachev resigned on 25 December 1991 and died in 2022.

His aim was to save and renew socialism, not to end it. As a participant he chose not to use force in eastern Europe, unlike Khrushchev in 1956, and most historians agree that the consequences, the end of communist rule and of the Union, were ones he did not foresee.

Contemporaries abroad welcomed him. After meeting him in December 1984 Margaret Thatcher said: 'I like Mr Gorbachev. We can do business together.' Reagan negotiated arms agreements with him, 'Gorbymania' (popular enthusiasm) swept the West, and he won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1990.

At home conservatives blamed him for destroying the system, radicals such as Yeltsin (dismissed in 1987 after attacking the slow pace of reform) thought him too slow, and many Russians blamed him for shortages and economic collapse.

Historians differ. Archie Brown (The Gorbachev Factor, 1996) sees a genuine transformer of the system; Stephen Kotkin (Armageddon Averted, 2001) argues the system was already doomed and that his achievement was that it ended without war.
notes.tip: Gorbachev is a frequent question: hold one judgement throughout (for example highly effective abroad, much less so at home), give dates for each step (1985, 1986, 1987, 1988, 1989, 1991), and pair each success with its limit. Unlike Khrushchev, he refused to use force.

notes.h: Why reform was needed: uskorenie and perestroika
notes.b: By 1985 the Soviet Union was stagnating, and Gorbachev set out to renew it from above. His economic policies moved from a simple push for speed to a wider restructuring, and neither cured the shortages.
points: Reform was needed because of economic stagnation, the cost of the arms race and of the war in Afghanistan (Soviet troops there since December 1979), and an ageing leadership.
World oil prices fell sharply in 1986, cutting Soviet export earnings, so the state had less money to meet its costs.
He relied on younger reformers, notably Alexander Yakovlev, his key adviser on reform and glasnost, and Eduard Shevardnadze, foreign minister from 1985.
His first economic slogan, in 1985-86, was uskorenie (acceleration of economic growth). It tried to speed up the existing planned economy, and when it failed he moved to perestroika.
The anti-alcohol campaign of May 1985 belonged to this early effort, but it was unpopular and cost the state tax revenue.

Perestroika (restructuring) set out to reform the economy, and later the political system, by adding limited market elements to central planning. The Law on State Enterprise (1987) gave factories more freedom over output and prices.
The Law on Cooperatives (1988) allowed small private businesses, for example restaurants and workshops, so private enterprise returned in a limited form.
Perestroika failed because it was a set of half-measures: markets were added but planning was not abandoned, so by 1990-91 there were empty shops, rationing, rising prices and falling output.
notes.tip: Do not confuse the terms: glasnost (openness), perestroika (restructuring), uskorenie (acceleration) and democratisation. Defining glasnost and perestroika correctly earns marks on its own.

notes.h: Glasnost and democratisation
notes.b: Gorbachev found that economic reform needed honest information and public pressure on officials. Glasnost opened up discussion, and democratisation then gave voters a real say.
points: Glasnost means openness: freer discussion, less censorship and criticism of officials and of the Soviet past. It was proclaimed at the 27th Party Congress in February-March 1986.

The reactor explosion at Chernobyl, in Soviet Ukraine (not Russia), on 26 April 1986 exposed the secrecy of the system: the authorities said nothing for about two days, until radiation was detected in Sweden. The concealment strengthened the case for glasnost.
Banned works were published, which showed the new openness, such as Boris Pasternak's Doctor Zhivago (1988) and Solzhenitsyn's writings (1989-90), and Stalin's crimes were openly discussed.
Dissidents (open critics of the regime) were released, for example the nuclear physicist Andrei Sakharov, freed from internal exile in Gorky in December 1986.
Democratisation (demokratizatsiya) meant partly free elections and the end of the party's monopoly of power.

The elections to the Congress of People's Deputies in March 1989 were the first partly free elections in the Soviet Union since 1917. Several party bosses were defeated and the sessions were televised.
In February-March 1990 the party gave up its leading role (Article 6 of the constitution was amended in March 1990), and in March 1990 Gorbachev became the first executive president of the USSR.
Glasnost also released nationalism in the republics, so the success of freeing speech carried a limit that Gorbachev could not control.
notes.tip: Pair each success with its limit: glasnost freeing speech against glasnost releasing nationalism. Chernobyl is the case that exposed secrecy.

notes.h: New thinking: arms control and the end of the Cold War
notes.b: Gorbachev wanted to cut the military burden that was crippling the economy. His 'new thinking' in foreign policy, helped by Shevardnadze, ended the arms race and eased tension with the West.
points: He held summits with Reagan at Geneva (November 1985), Reykjavik (October 1986) and Washington (December 1987). At Reykjavik they came close to agreeing deep cuts in nuclear weapons but failed over SDI.

The INF Treaty, signed in Washington on 8 December 1987, abolished all US and Soviet intermediate-range (500-5,500 km) land-based missiles, the first treaty to remove a whole class of nuclear weapons.

In his United Nations General Assembly speech on 7 December 1988 he announced that Soviet armed forces would be cut by 500,000 men and some divisions withdrawn from eastern Europe, which signalled a lower military threat.
The last Soviet troops left Afghanistan on 15 February 1989, ending a costly war that had begun in December 1979, so the USSR no longer had to pay for it.
At the Malta summit with President George H. W. Bush on 2-3 December 1989 (Bush, not Reagan) the leaders met as the bloc collapsed, and it is often seen as marking the end of the Cold War.
START I (strategic arms reduction) was signed in July 1991 to cut the long-range nuclear weapons of both sides, which continued arms control after the INF Treaty.
notes.tip: Do not mix up the summits: Geneva 1985, Reykjavik 1986, Washington 1987 (INF), Malta 1989 (Bush). Questions on how the Cold War ended reward linking each step to the easing of tension.

notes.h: The revolutions of 1989: Poland and Hungary
notes.b: In 1989 communist rule collapsed across eastern Europe in a few months, almost entirely without Soviet intervention. Poland and Hungary went first, and Hungary's actions opened a route to the West for East Germans.
points: The Polish elections of 4 and 18 June 1989 were not fully free, because a set share of Sejm seats was reserved for the communists and their allies. Solidarity won all but one of the Sejm seats it could contest (161) and 99 of the 100 Senate seats.

Jaruzelski was elected president by parliament in July 1989. In August 1989 Tadeusz Mazowiecki, a Catholic journalist and Solidarity adviser, became prime minister of the first non-communist-led government in the Soviet bloc in over forty years.
Wałęsa was elected President of Poland in December 1990.

In Hungary János Kádár, leader since 1956, was removed in May 1988. The dismantling of the border fence with Austria began on 2 May 1989, and on 27 June the Hungarian and Austrian foreign ministers, Gyula Horn and Alois Mock, cut the wire publicly.

Imre Nagy, leader of the 1956 uprising, was reburied with honours in Budapest on 16 June 1989 before a huge crowd, which turned the memory of 1956 into a national symbol and a challenge to the regime.

At the Pan-European Picnic near Sopron on 19 August 1989 several hundred East Germans crossed to Austria, and on 11 September 1989 Hungary opened its border to East Germans so that they could escape west.

Round-table talks agreed multi-party elections, the party renamed itself the Hungarian Socialist Party in October 1989, and the Republic of Hungary was proclaimed on 23 October 1989, the anniversary of 1956.
Free elections in March-April 1990 were won by the Hungarian Democratic Forum, and József Antall became prime minister.
notes.tip: Ordinary Level questions ask why Hungary's opening of its border mattered: East Germans escaped west. Do not call the 1989 Polish elections fully free, and do not confuse Imre Nagy with Ferenc Nagy.

notes.h: The revolutions of 1989: East Germany and the Berlin Wall
notes.b: East Germany's government collapsed under pressure from its own people, who first left in thousands and then marched. The opening of the Berlin Wall became the symbol of the end of the division of Europe.
points: Thousands of East Germans fled through Hungary and Czechoslovakia and camped in the West German embassy in Prague, until they were allowed to leave for the West at the end of September 1989.

New Forum, an opposition group, was founded in September 1989, and the Leipzig Monday demonstrations began that month. On 9 October about 70,000 marched and the security forces did not fire, which showed that the regime had lost the will to shoot.
Gorbachev attended the GDR's 40th anniversary celebrations on 7 October 1989 and urged reform, a sign that Moscow would not back the hardliners with force.
Erich Honecker, East German leader since 1971, resigned on 18 October 1989 because the demonstrations could not be stopped, and Egon Krenz succeeded him.
A mass rally in East Berlin on 4 November 1989 followed. The slogan 'We are the people' later became 'We are one people', showing the shift from demanding reform to demanding unity.

On the evening of 9 November 1989 Günter Schabowski, Politburo spokesman, told a press conference that new travel rules applied 'immediately'. The announcement was confused, and crowds gathered at the crossings.
Guards at Bornholmer Strasse opened the gate that night, so the Wall was opened, not knocked down; demolition came in 1990.
notes.tip: Say the Wall was opened on 9 November 1989, not knocked down. Ordinary Level questions may ask you to recognise the opening of the Wall in a photograph or cartoon.

notes.h: The revolutions of 1989: Czechoslovakia, Bulgaria and Romania
notes.b: The last regimes fell in a rush in November and December 1989. Czechoslovakia's change was peaceful, Bulgaria's came from inside the party, and Romania's was the only violent revolution of 1989.
points: The Velvet Revolution began on 17 November 1989, when police beat a student march in Prague. It is called 'velvet' because it was peaceful.
Mass demonstrations and a general strike on 27 November followed. Civic Forum, with Havel, led the opposition in the Czech lands, and Public Against Violence did so in Slovakia.
The party gave up its leading role at the end of November, and Husák resigned as president in December 1989.
Dubček was elected chairman of the Federal Assembly on 28 December and Václav Havel president on 29 December 1989, so the leader of 1968 and the Charter 77 spokesman stood together at the end.
In Bulgaria, Todor Zhivkov, leader since 1954, was removed by his own party on 10 November 1989 and replaced by Petar Mladenov.
In Romania protests began in Timișoara on 16 December 1989 over the eviction of the Hungarian Protestant pastor László Tőkés, and security forces fired on the crowds.
A rally in Bucharest on 21 December turned against Nicolae Ceaușescu. He fled by helicopter on 22 December, the army changed sides, and there was fighting with Securitate (secret police) loyalists.
The National Salvation Front, led by Ion Iliescu, took power. Nicolae and Elena Ceaușescu were tried by a military court and shot on 25 December 1989. About 1,100 people died in the revolution.
notes.tip: The Velvet Revolution (Czechoslovakia, 1989) and the velvet divorce (the split of Czechoslovakia, 1993) are different events. Romania is the only violent revolution of 1989.

notes.h: Why the revolutions of 1989 happened together and peacefully
notes.b: The speed and calm of 1989 need explaining, because earlier risings had been crushed. The central change was that Moscow no longer backed its allies with force.
points: In October 1989 Gennady Gerasimov, the Soviet foreign ministry spokesman, said the Brezhnev Doctrine had been replaced by the 'Sinatra Doctrine' (after the song 'My Way'), meaning that eastern European states could choose their own path.
Non-intervention was Gorbachev's choice. He meant to renew socialism, not to free eastern Europe, so the fall of the regimes was a consequence he did not foresee.
The economic failure of the regimes had already cost them public support, so there was little loyalty left to defend them.
Each neighbour's example mattered: success in Poland and Hungary showed that change was possible, which encouraged protesters in East Germany and Czechoslovakia.
Television and travel showed eastern Europeans the prosperity of the West, which made their own living standards look worse.
The regimes lost the will to shoot because they knew Soviet tanks would not come, so the police and army did not fire on the crowds.
notes.tip: Rank the causes of 1989 rather than list them: Soviet non-intervention was the trigger, set against economic failure and the example of neighbours. Do not mix up the Brezhnev Doctrine (1968, intervention) and the Sinatra Doctrine (1989, non-intervention).

notes.h: Nationalism in the republics and the rise of Yeltsin, 1988-1991
notes.b: Glasnost let the republics of the USSR (the Soviet Union was a federation of fifteen republics) air grievances that had long been suppressed. National demands and a rival leader in Russia weakened Gorbachev's authority.
points: Nagorno-Karabakh was the scene of an Armenian-Azerbaijani conflict from 1988, which showed that glasnost let old ethnic quarrels resurface.
In Tbilisi, Georgia, in April 1989, troops killed peaceful demonstrators, which hardened nationalist feeling.
On 23 August 1989, the 50th anniversary of the Nazi-Soviet Pact, about two million people formed a human chain across Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania, called the Baltic Way.

Lithuania, led by Vytautas Landsbergis, declared independence on 11 March 1990, and other Soviet republics followed in demanding sovereignty. In January 1991 Soviet troops killed fourteen people at the Vilnius television tower.

Boris Yeltsin, Moscow party chief, attacked the slow pace of reform and was dismissed in 1987. He was elected chairman of the Russian parliament in May 1990, left the Communist Party in 1990, and Russia declared its sovereignty in June 1990.
On 12 June 1991 Yeltsin was elected President of the Russian republic by popular vote. This gave him a mandate Gorbachev lacked and made Russian sovereignty a rival to Soviet authority.
notes.tip: Do not say Gorbachev was elected by the people: Yeltsin was the one with a popular mandate (June 1991). Lithuania declared independence in March 1990, but recognition came in September 1991.

notes.h: The August coup and the end of the bloc, 1991
notes.b: In 1991 the institutions of the Soviet system fell apart one after another. A coup by hardliners meant to save the Union instead hastened its end.
points: Comecon was dissolved in June 1991 and the Warsaw Pact was formally dissolved on 1 July 1991 in Prague. Soviet troops left Hungary and Czechoslovakia in 1991, and the last left Germany in 1994.
The coup of 19-21 August 1991 came on the eve of a new Union Treaty giving the republics more power, which hardliners feared would break up the Union.

It was staged by the State Committee for the State of Emergency, eight hardliners including Vice-President Gennady Yanayev, KGB chairman Vladimir Kryuchkov and Defence Minister Dmitry Yazov. Gorbachev was held at his holiday home at Foros, Crimea.
Yeltsin spoke from a tank outside the Russian parliament (the White House) in Moscow and rallied opposition. Troops would not attack, three civilians were killed, and the coup collapsed.
Gorbachev returned on 22 August, weakened, and resigned as General Secretary on 24 August 1991. The Communist Party was suspended, and Yeltsin banned it in Russia in November 1991.
The republics declared independence. The USSR recognised Estonian, Latvian and Lithuanian independence on 6 September 1991, and all three were admitted to the UN on 17 September 1991.
notes.tip: Date the coup 19-21 August 1991 and name its committee. It failed after Yeltsin rallied opposition, and it accelerated the break-up of the union.

notes.h: The dissolution of the USSR, December 1991
notes.b: After the coup the Union had no authority left, and the republics negotiated their way out. The end came in a few weeks.
points: On 1 December 1991 Ukraine held an independence referendum with about 90 per cent in favour, which made it hard to keep the Union together.

On 8 December 1991 the leaders of Russia, Ukraine and Belarus met at Belovezha (the Minsk agreement), declared the USSR at an end and founded the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS), a loose association of former republics.
More republics joined the CIS at Alma-Ata on 21 December 1991, so the CIS replaced the Union.
Gorbachev resigned as Soviet president on 25 December 1991 because the Union he led no longer existed in practice, and the red flag over the Kremlin was lowered that evening.
The USSR was formally dissolved on 26 December 1991, a day after his resignation, leaving fifteen independent successor states.
notes.tip: Gorbachev resigned on 25 December 1991, but the USSR ended formally on 26 December; do not run the two together.

notes.h: German reunification, 1989-1990
notes.b: The fall of the Wall put unity on the agenda within weeks. Chancellor Helmut Kohl moved quickly, and Gorbachev's consent allowed a united Germany to remain in NATO.
points: Helmut Kohl, West German chancellor from 1982 to 1998, pushed for rapid unity after the Wall fell, so he set out a Ten-Point Plan on 28 November 1989.
In the first free East German election on 18 March 1990 the Kohl-backed Alliance for Germany won, and Lothar de Maizière became prime minister, which showed that East Germans wanted unity.
Monetary, economic and social union came into force on 1 July 1990, so that the Deutsche Mark became East Germany's currency.
In July 1990 Gorbachev accepted that a united Germany could be in NATO, in return for German aid and limits on German forces.
The Two Plus Four Treaty was signed in Moscow on 12 September 1990 by the two German states plus the USA, the Soviet Union, Britain and France.
It gave Germany full sovereignty, confirmed the Oder-Neisse border, left a united Germany free to stay in NATO and required Soviet troops to leave.
Unification took place on 3 October 1990, when the territory of the GDR joined the Federal Republic. Kohl won the first all-German election in December 1990.
notes.tip: Keep the dates apart: currency union 1 July 1990, Two Plus Four Treaty 12 September 1990, unification 3 October 1990.

notes.h: The break-up of Yugoslavia, 1991-1992
notes.b: Yugoslavia was a federation of republics held together under Tito. When communism fell, nationalism broke it apart, and unlike most of 1989 the change was violent.
points: Tito died in May 1980, and a rotating collective presidency followed, so no single leader held the federation together. Economic crisis and rising nationalism followed.
Slobodan Milošević, Serbian leader from 1987 (president of Serbia from 1989), stirred Serb nationalism, and from 1991 Serbia opposed the secession of Slovenia and Croatia.
Slovenia and Croatia declared independence on 25 June 1991, and Macedonia declared independence in 1991 too.
The Ten-Day War in Slovenia (June-July 1991) ended with the Yugoslav army withdrawing, so Slovenia's break was brief.
War in Croatia began in 1991 because Serbia opposed secession, with the siege and fall of Vukovar in November 1991.
The European Community recognised Slovenia and Croatia on 15 January 1992, after Germany pressed for it.
Bosnia-Herzegovina voted for independence in a referendum in February-March 1992, boycotted by most Bosnian Serbs, and was recognised in April 1992. War and the siege of Sarajevo began that month.
The war in Bosnia lasted until 1995 and was the bloodiest in Europe since 1945.

notes.h: Realignment: central Europe, the Baltic states and Czechoslovakia
notes.b: With the Soviet bloc gone, the former satellites and the Baltic states looked west, Czechoslovakia split peacefully, and the CIS took shape in the east.
points: The Visegrád group of Poland, Czechoslovakia and Hungary, which was founded on 15 February 1991, coordinated their approach to integration with the West.

The former satellites and the Baltic states turned to Western institutions: the Council of Europe, the European Community and NATO. Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic later joined NATO in 1999, and most of them and the Baltic states joined the EU in 2004.
Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania regained independence in 1991 and sought membership of Western institutions.
In the east the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) linked former Soviet republics loosely, so Russia kept some influence without the old Union.

Czechoslovakia divided peacefully into the Czech Republic and Slovakia on 1 January 1993, agreed in 1992 after the June elections won by Vladimír Mečiar's party in Slovakia and Václav Klaus's in the Czech lands.
notes.tip: Do not confuse the Velvet Revolution of 1989 with the velvet divorce of 1993, which was the peaceful split.

notes.h: Assessment: Gorbachev's successes and failures
notes.b: Examiners reward a judgement that weighs what Gorbachev achieved against what he lost. His record was far stronger abroad than at home.
points: Success abroad: the INF Treaty, the UN troop cuts and START I ended the arms race. Failure at home: the economy got worse, with empty shops, rationing and falling output by 1990-91.

Success: the withdrawal from Afghanistan in February 1989 ended a costly war, which freed money and effort for reform. Limit: shortages made him unpopular at home, so foreign admiration did not translate into support.

Success: non-intervention let eastern Europe change peacefully and let Germany unite within NATO. Failure: the loss of the Union he meant to save, as nationalism grew in the republics and the August 1991 coup failed.
Success: glasnost brought freedom of speech and partly free elections. Limit: it released nationalism, and he reformed the party's monopoly of power too slowly to keep control.
Contemporary views: Western leaders welcomed him, while conservatives at home blamed him for destroying the system and radicals such as Yeltsin for being too slow.
Later views: Archie Brown credits him as a genuine transformer, while Stephen Kotkin argues the system was already doomed and that his achievement was that it ended without war.
Compared with Khrushchev, Gorbachev also reformed from above, met resistance and fell, but unlike Khrushchev he refused to use force, and his reforms ended the bloc and the Union.
notes.tip: Pair a success with its limit in each paragraph: arms control against economic collapse, glasnost against nationalism, non-intervention against losing the Union.

notes.h: Assessment: why did communism collapse?
notes.b: Historians explain the collapse through long-term failure, short-term triggers and the decision not to use force. The best answers rank these causes and weigh internal against external ones.
points: Long-term causes: the command economy failed to deliver, and the regimes lacked legitimacy because they had never ruled by consent. Nationalism, the burden of the arms race, which the West pressed on through defence spending, and Western prosperity seen on television added to the pressure.
Short-term causes: Gorbachev's reforms and non-intervention removed the threat of Soviet force, which had held the regimes up since 1953.
Opposition movements such as Solidarity and Charter 77, and the Church, kept reform alive through repression, and the domino effect of 1989 carried change from one country to the next.
Internal view: Stephen Kotkin and others stress the structural weakness of the system, while Archie Brown stresses Gorbachev's personal role.

External view: contemporary Western conservatives credited Reagan's pressure, including the arms build-up, SDI and his 'tear down this wall' speech in Berlin in June 1987. This is one view, not proven fact, and later historians give more weight to the Soviet system's internal crisis.
Soviet control of eastern Europe was kept by force in 1953, 1956 and 1968 and by proxy in 1981, but never by consent, and it was lost within months once Moscow would not use force.
notes.tip: Rank the causes instead of listing them, weigh internal against external (Reagan) causes and name historians' views. For control of eastern Europe, give a balanced judgement with each crisis dated: success in holding power, failure in winning consent.

keyTerms.definition: Gorbachev's policy of greater openness in public life, including freer discussion of the Soviet past and criticism of officials.
A political and economic system in which a single communist party directs the state and the economy is publicly owned and centrally planned.
Gorbachev's programme to restructure the Soviet economy, introducing limited market mechanisms within a planned system.
The 1968 reform movement in Czechoslovakia under Alexander Dubček, which was ended by a Warsaw Pact invasion on 20–21 August 1968.
The Soviet claim, set out in 1968, that socialist states had the right to intervene when socialism was threatened in another socialist state.
The independent trade union founded at the Gdańsk shipyard in 1980, which became a mass opposition movement in Poland.
The informal name for Gorbachev's policy of not intervening in eastern Europe, so that each state could choose its own path.
The peaceful overthrow of communist rule in Czechoslovakia in November and December 1989.
The policy in Czechoslovakia after 1968, under Husák, of reversing the Prague Spring reforms and purging reformers.
A declaration by Czechoslovak dissidents in January 1977 that demanded respect for the human rights guaranteed in the Helsinki Final Act.
The talks between the Polish government and Solidarity from February to April 1989 that led to semi-free elections.
The end of the Soviet Union on 26 December 1991, after the August coup, leaving fifteen independent republics.

factCards.definition: Workers protested against wage increases and shortages, and Soviet tanks suppressed the uprising in East Berlin.
The Prague Spring's Action Programme of April 1968 proposed freedom of expression and a looser press.

factCards.term: Warsaw Pact invasion of Czechoslovakia: date
factCards.definition: Forces from five Warsaw Pact states invaded on 20–21 August 1968 and arrested Dubček.
A declaration by Czechoslovak dissidents issued in January 1977 and led by Václav Havel.
Signed on 31 August 1980, it recognised the right to form independent trade unions in Poland.
General Wojciech Jaruzelski declared martial law on 13 December 1981 and banned Solidarity.
Tadeusz Mazowiecki became prime minister of the first non-communist government in the Soviet bloc since 1948.
The Wall was opened on 9 November 1989 after a confused announcement about travel rules.
Nicolae Ceaușescu and his wife were executed on 25 December 1989 after a violent uprising in Romania.
A reactor exploded on 26 April 1986 in Soviet Ukraine, and the official response was criticised for concealment.
Signed on 8 December 1987, it eliminated US and Soviet intermediate-range nuclear missiles.
The USSR was dissolved on 26 December 1991, a day after Gorbachev resigned as president.
The two German states were unified on 3 October 1990.
Glasnost (openness), perestroika (restructuring of the economy) and democratisation, including the partly free elections of 1989.

factCards.term: Why did communism collapse? Four causes
factCards.definition: The failure of the command economy, the cost of the arms race and Afghanistan, Gorbachev's decision not to use force, and the strength of opposition movements.
